# Hypotheses

**H1:** Individualistic attitudes (DV) will be stronger among full-time employed individuals than among unemployed individuals (IV).

**H2:** Gender-equality attitudes (DV) will be associated with daily time spent enhancing appearance (IV).

## 1. Load the package and data

```{r load, message=FALSE}
library(codebook)

raw <- read.csv("data/raw/data_doctored.csv")

# Check the dimensions, participant IDs, and variable structure
dim(raw)
head(raw$ResponseId)
str(raw)

# Keep only variables needed for H1 and H2
data <- raw[, c(
  "ResponseId",
  "Gender_Equality_1", "Gender_Equality_2", "Gender_Equality_3",
  "Time_A_makeup_1", "Time_A_hyg_1", "Time_A_cosm_1",
  "Time_A_exercise_1", "Time_A_hair_1", "Time_A_dress_1",
  "Time_A_diet_1", "Time_A_other_1",
  "Individualism_col_1", "Individualism_col_2",
  "Individualism_col_4", "Employment"
)]
```

## 2. Validate participant IDs

Check for missing, blank, and duplicated participant IDs. Remove rows without a usable participant ID.

```{r participant_ids}
# Count missing IDs
sum(is.na(data$ResponseId))

# Count blank IDs
sum(trimws(data$ResponseId) == "", na.rm = TRUE)

# Count duplicated IDs
sum(duplicated(data$ResponseId))

# Remove rows with missing or blank IDs
data <- data[
  !is.na(data$ResponseId) & trimws(data$ResponseId) != "",
]

# Check the dimensions after cleaning
dim(data)
```

# Hypothesis 1: Individualism and employment

## 3. Validate and recode employment

The Employment variable allows multiple selections. Create separate indicators for full-time employment and unemployment. Participants who selected both categories are treated as having conflicting responses and excluded from the comparison.

```{r employment}
# Identify missing or blank responses
missing_employment <- is.na(data$Employment) |
  trimws(data$Employment) == ""

# Identify participants who selected both categories
both_selected <- grepl("(^|,)1(,|$)", data$Employment) &
  grepl("(^|,)4(,|$)", data$Employment)

# Create the full-time employment indicator
data$Full_time <- ifelse(
  missing_employment | both_selected,
  NA,
  as.integer(grepl("(^|,)1(,|$)", data$Employment))
)

# Create the unemployment indicator
data$Unemployed <- ifelse(
  missing_employment | both_selected,
  NA,
  as.integer(grepl("(^|,)4(,|$)", data$Employment))
)

# Check how many participants selected both categories
sum(both_selected, na.rm = TRUE)

# Check the two indicators
table(data$Full_time, useNA = "ifany")
table(data$Unemployed, useNA = "ifany")

# Check whether anyone is coded as both
table(data$Full_time, data$Unemployed, useNA = "ifany")
```

## 4. Validate and score individualistic attitudes

Use Individualism items 1, 2, and 4. Convert responses to numeric values, treat special missing codes as missing, check the valid response range, and reverse-code the items. Higher composite scores represent greater individualism.

```{r individualism}
# Select the three individualism items
ind_var <- c(
  "Individualism_col_1",
  "Individualism_col_2",
  "Individualism_col_4"
)

# Inspect example responses and original variable types
lapply(data[ind_var], head)
sapply(data[ind_var], class)

# Convert responses to numeric and handle missing codes
data[ind_var] <- lapply(data[ind_var], function(x) {
  x <- trimws(x)
  x[x %in% c("", "-99", "N/A")] <- NA
  as.numeric(x)
})

# Check for invalid responses outside 1-7 or not whole numbers
sapply(data[ind_var], function(x) {
  sum(!is.na(x) & (x < 1 | x > 7 | x != floor(x)))
})

# Set invalid responses to missing
data[ind_var] <- lapply(data[ind_var], function(x) {
  invalid <- !is.na(x) &
    (x < 1 | x > 7 | x != floor(x))
  x[invalid] <- NA
  x
})

# Reverse-code the items: 1 becomes 7, 2 becomes 6, etc.
data[paste0(ind_var, "_R")] <- 8 - data[ind_var]

# Calculate the mean; missing items result in a missing composite
data$ind_rev_mean <- rowMeans(
  data[paste0(ind_var, "_R")],
  na.rm = FALSE
)

# Inspect the composite scores
summary(data$ind_rev_mean)
```

## 5. Create the H1 analysis dataset

Create one employment-group variable so that only full-time employed and unemployed participants are included. Participants in other employment categories, with missing employment information, or with conflicting responses are excluded.

```{r h1_data}
###JK: Great work with this code! Just clarify the group descriptions. ###
# Your code includes people who selected Full-time plus another option, such as Student.
# Please say that additional selections are allowed, but selecting both Full-time and Unemployed leads to exclusion.
# No code change is needed.
###  End of comment ###

# Create the two-group employment variable
data$Employment_group <- ifelse(
  data$Full_time == 1,
  "Full-time",
  ifelse(data$Unemployed == 1, "Unemployed", NA)
)

# Keep participants with valid scores in the two comparison groups
h1_data <- data[
  !is.na(data$ind_rev_mean) &
    !is.na(data$Employment_group),
  c("ResponseId", "Employment_group", "ind_rev_mean")
]

# Set the order of the employment groups
h1_data$Employment_group <- factor(
  h1_data$Employment_group,
  levels = c("Unemployed", "Full-time")
)

# Check the final H1 dataset
dim(h1_data)
head(h1_data)
table(h1_data$Employment_group, useNA = "ifany")
colSums(is.na(h1_data))
```

# Hypothesis 2: Gender equality and appearance time

## 6. Validate and score gender-equality attitudes

Convert the three gender-equality items to numeric values, handle missing codes, and check the valid response range. The items are reverse-coded so higher scores indicate stronger gender-equality endorsement, as confirmed against the codebook.

```{r gender_equality}
# Select the three gender-equality items
ge_var <- c(
  "Gender_Equality_1",
  "Gender_Equality_2",
  "Gender_Equality_3"
)

# Inspect the original response values
lapply(raw[ge_var], function(x) sort(unique(x)))

# Convert responses to numeric and handle missing codes
data[ge_var] <- lapply(data[ge_var], function(x) {
  x <- trimws(x)
  x[x %in% c("", "-99", "N/A")] <- NA
  as.numeric(x)
})

# Check for invalid responses outside 1-7 or not whole numbers
sapply(data[ge_var], function(x) {
  sum(!is.na(x) & (x < 1 | x > 7 | x != floor(x)))
})

# Set invalid responses to missing
data[ge_var] <- lapply(data[ge_var], function(x) {
  invalid <- !is.na(x) &
    (x < 1 | x > 7 | x != floor(x))
  x[invalid] <- NA
  x
})

# Reverse-code the items
data[paste0(ge_var, "_R")] <- 8 - data[ge_var]

# Calculate the mean; missing items result in a missing composite
data$Gender_Equality_mean <- rowMeans(
  data[paste0(ge_var, "_R")],
  na.rm = FALSE
)

# Inspect the composite scores
summary(data$Gender_Equality_mean)
```

## 7. Validate and score appearance-enhancement time

The eight variables measure minutes per day spent on appearance-related activities. A value of 360 represents six hours or more for an individual activity and is retained as valid. The total is calculated only when all eight activity responses are available.

```{r appearance_time}
# Select the eight appearance-time items
time_var <- c(
  "Time_A_makeup_1",
  "Time_A_hyg_1",
  "Time_A_cosm_1",
  "Time_A_exercise_1",
  "Time_A_hair_1",
  "Time_A_dress_1",
  "Time_A_diet_1",
  "Time_A_other_1"
)

# Check variable types
sapply(data[time_var], class)

# Count invalid values below 0 or above 360
sapply(data[time_var], function(x) {
  sum(!is.na(x) & (x < 0 | x > 360))
})

# Set invalid values to missing
data[time_var] <- lapply(data[time_var], function(x) {
  invalid <- !is.na(x) & (x < 0 | x > 360)
  x[invalid] <- NA
  x
})

# Calculate total daily appearance-enhancement time
data$Appearance_time_total <- rowSums(
  data[time_var],
  na.rm = FALSE
)

# Inspect the total scores
summary(data$Appearance_time_total)
```

## 8. Create the H2 analysis dataset

Keep participants who have complete scores for both gender-equality attitudes and total appearance-enhancement time.

```{r h2_data}
h2_data <- data[
  !is.na(data$Gender_Equality_mean) &
    !is.na(data$Appearance_time_total),
  c(
    "ResponseId",
    "Gender_Equality_mean",
    "Appearance_time_total"
  )
]

```

# 9. Add variable labels

The labels describe what each variable measures, how composite scores are calculated, and the relevant units. Keep the labels in the same order as the columns.

```{r variable_labels}
# Labels for H1
var_label(h1_data) <- c(
  "Unique participant ID (ResponseId)",
  "Employment comparison group: Full-time or Unemployed; other employment categories and missing or conflicting responses are excluded",
  "Individualistic attitudes: mean of Individualism_col_1, Individualism_col_2, and Individualism_col_4 after reverse-coding each item as 8-x; higher scores indicate greater individualism"
)

# Labels for H2
var_label(h2_data) <- c(
  "Unique participant ID (ResponseId)",
  "Gender-equality attitudes: mean of Gender_Equality_1, Gender_Equality_2, and Gender_Equality_3 after reverse-coding each item as 8-x; higher scores indicate stronger gender-equality endorsement",
  "Daily time spent enhancing appearance: sum of eight Time_A variables covering makeup, hygiene, cosmetics, exercise, hair, dress, diet, and other activities; minutes per day; 360 represents six hours or more for an individual activity"
)
```

```{r}

# Create the output folder if it does not already exist
if (!dir.exists("data/processed_data")) {
  dir.create("data/processed_data", recursive = TRUE)
}

# Save the cleaned H1 and H2 datasets
write.csv(
  h1_data,
  "data/processed_data/practice_h1.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  h2_data,
  "data/processed_data/practice_h2.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

# Read the files back in to verify they were saved
h1Saved <- read.csv("data/processed_data/practice_h1.csv")
h2Saved <- read.csv("data/processed_data/practice_h2.csv")

# Check dimensions and missing values
dim(h1Saved)
dim(h2Saved)

colSums(is.na(h1Saved))
colSums(is.na(h2Saved))

```
